forces: Trumpets, horns, oboes, bassoon, strings and continuo
performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Major Michelle Rakers, conductor
intro: The Allegro opens Handel’s Water Music Suite No. 2 in D, HWV 349. Trumpets begin with a fanfare and the horns follow over a running bass, and the two groups play separately until the whole orchestra takes up one tune.

sections.label: A · Trumpets call, horns answer
sections.mNote: Fanfare, quick string replies, then horns over the bass

sections.label: B · Short chords after a pause
sections.mNote: The orchestra plays short detached chords and rising figures.

sections.label: C · Trumpets lead, D major
sections.mNote: Oboes and violins play D major arpeggios.

sections.label: D · Short phrases exchanged between brass groups
sections.mNote: The two groups alternate bar by bar

sections.label: C′ · Trumpet passage returns
sections.mNote: Trumpets, arpeggios, then horns with bassoon and continuo.

sections.label: E · The whole orchestra together
sections.mNote: One dotted tune above running strings and bass

sections.label: Coda · Adagio for strings
sections.mNote: The winds rest; six slower string chords end the movement.

cues.title: Opening, trumpets and horns
cues.text: The trumpets play first. Oboes and strings follow with quick semiquavers, and then the horns enter, with bassoon and bass running beneath them. While one group plays, Handel keeps the others silent.
cues.evidence: Samuel Arnold’s full score, The Celebrated Water-musick (1788), p. 35; Allegro, bars 1–8 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(19_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing tutti
cues.text: In the closing passage, trumpets, horns, oboes, second violins and violas play a dotted tune together. First violins play semiquavers around it, and the bass keeps moving.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 38–39; Allegro, bars 37–47 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. The established section boundary marks the closing tutti. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(21_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing Adagio for strings
cues.text: After the brass finish, Handel adds a short Adagio for strings and continuo, with rests in all the wind parts. It consists of six slow chords. The first violins play A♯ and D♯.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 39: closing Adagio, with rests in all wind parts and chromatic first-violin notes; bars 48–50 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(21_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Rests after the horn fanfare
transitions.to: B · Short chords after a pause
transitions.how: The horns finish their fanfare over moving bassoon and bass. Rests follow, and then the orchestra returns with short D major chords and rising figures. Trumpets and horns now play the same phrase as the oboes and strings.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 35–36; Allegro, bars 5–11 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. The score shows the horn-and-bass passage, rests and fuller scoring.

transitions.title: Trumpets lead the next phrase
transitions.from: B · Short chords after a pause
transitions.how: The short chordal exchange ends with another rest. The trumpets lead the next phrase, and the oboes and violins reply with D major arpeggios while the bass rests. The horns then take over, with bassoon and continuo moving beneath them.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 36–37; Allegro, bars 15–21 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe: trumpet phrase, arpeggios above a resting bass, then horns and bassoon.

transitions.title: Exchanges shorten to one bar each
transitions.to: D · Short phrases exchanged between brass groups
transitions.how: In bars 22–28 the horns finish their phrase over running bass quavers. Trumpets, oboes and upper strings follow with a short turning figure, and the figure passes straight back to the horns and bass. The exchanges between the two groups shorten to one bar each, and the Allegro pulse continues through each change of group.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 37; Allegro, bars 22–28 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. Alternating scoring shortens the exchanges between the two groups.

transitions.title: The trumpet phrase returns
transitions.from: D · Short phrases exchanged between brass groups
transitions.how: The trumpet-led passage returns in D major in bars 29–36, repeating the pattern of bars 15–22. Oboes and violins again play arpeggios while the bass rests, then the horns enter over bassoon and continuo. The quick string figures come between these entries in the same order as before.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 37–38; Allegro, bars 29–36 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe repeat the trumpet, arpeggio and horn pattern of bars 15–22.

transitions.title: Horns, then the whole orchestra
transitions.how: In bars 35–38 (Hallische Händel-Ausgabe), the horns play above the running bassoon and continuo while the trumpets, oboes and strings rest. The full orchestra then enters with the dotted D major tune. First violins add semiquavers, and the bass continues its running line beneath the brass.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 38; Allegro, bars 35–38 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe: horn-and-bass writing followed by the tutti.

transitions.title: From D major tutti to string Adagio
transitions.how: The D major tutti ends with short chords separated by rests. Handel marks the remaining passage for strings and continuo Adagio, with six chords spread across three bars. Trumpets, horns and oboes are silent. The first violins introduce A♯ and D♯ into the slow-moving harmony.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 39; Allegro, bars 45–50 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe: separated tutti chords followed by the string Adagio.

source.title: Handel, The Celebrated Water-musick in score (London: Samuel Arnold, 1788), pp. 35–39
source.locator: Arnold’s full score, pp. 35–39, Commons images 19–21. Bar numbers follow the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe, IV/13 (1962), pp. 39–43. The trumpet-and-horn exchanges lead to a tutti at bar 37 and a string-and-continuo Adagio at bars 48–50.

timeline.note: Trumpets give the fanfare; oboes, violins and viola echo it in semiquavers (bars 1–4).
Horns restate the fanfare while bassoon and continuo run beneath; trumpets, oboes and violins rest (bars 5–8).
After the pause every section plays short chords and rising figures (bars 9–11).
One bar for trumpets, oboes and upper strings; horns and bass rest (bar 12).
Horns answer with bassoon and continuo (bars 13–14).
Trumpets restart; strings and bass join in the next bar (bars 15–16).
Trumpets hold a dotted tune while oboes and violins run D major arpeggios; the bass rests (bars 17–18).
Horns again, with bassoon and continuo in running quavers (bars 19–21).
Trumpets, oboes and upper strings exchange short phrases with horns and bass, bar by bar (bars 23–28).
The earlier pattern returns, with trumpets and strings first (bars 29–30).
Arpeggios in oboes and violins under the trumpets’ tune; the bass rests (bars 31–32).
Horns take their turn with bassoon and continuo; they are alone with the bass in bars 35–36 (bars 33–36).
The whole orchestra plays one dotted tune; first violins and low strings add running figures (bars 37–47).
Rests separate the last tutti chord from the string Adagio.
Adagio: strings and continuo play six chords while the winds rest (bars 48–50).

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor)
fields.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. A harpsichord, strings with a double bass, a bassoon and a trumpet are visible in the Marine Band’s video frames; horns and oboes could not be identified there.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (11 of the three suites), the 50 bars and the closing string-only Adagio match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
fields.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The numbering 11–15 for this suite follows the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962) and IMSLP; other editions may agree. The recording plays the closing Adagio (bars 48–50, strings only): about six soft chord attacks, roughly three seconds apart, follow the last tutti chord, and the official video shows the violins playing at about 1:46–2:00. The stretch is identified from the score, the six level peaks and the video, not by listening; whether anything else is audible after the last chord has not been checked by ear.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Commons gives performance_date 2017-01-29; the programme prints Sunday, January 29, 2017 at 2:00 P.M.; the official video description repeats the date. The Handel group stands after the intermission in the programme. The Commons composition_date field, 1717-07-17, is the date of the documented first performance on the Thames, not a composition date.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Handel (died 1759): the composition is in the public domain.
fields.note: Commons tags the composition PD-old-auto-expired (death year 1759). The performing edition is not identified; editorial copyright in a modern edition, if one was used, is separate from the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Commons tags the performance and recording PD-USGov-Military-Marines: a work of a United States Marine or employee made as part of official duties, public domain as a work of the U.S. federal government.
fields.note: This is a U.S.-jurisdiction statement, not a claim of worldwide status. The programme carries a general notice that a performance may contain third-party material and should not be assumed to be public domain; no third-party material is identified in this performance of a composition from before 1759, but the notice is recorded here. The official Marine Band YouTube channel published the source video.

composer.epithet: Composer who filled London theatres with Italian opera and later put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg had a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant, and Prince Ruspoli provided him with singers and instrumentalists to write for. In the Dixit Dominus of 1707, a setting of a Latin psalm, five choral parts move at speed, then some voices hold dissonant notes while the others move underneath. He wrote chamber cantatas for a single singer. In Corelli’s Rome he learned to write for violin alongside the voice.
